author: ChuckJones
title: Apple’s (NASDAQ: AAPL ) 10-Q filing contains a number of fin
text:
Apple’s (NASDAQ: AAPL ) 10-Q filing contains a number of financial details that provides additional information about what transpired in the most recent quarter and what the future may hold. When digging into it, you can see what gross margin would be without the accrued warranty expense, which is a “cleaner” number on how much it costs the company to provide its products and services and the operating profit margins for the five geographies. Apple also lets you know what interest rate it actually earns on its cash and investments and how much in components and products it has committed to buy from its manufacturing partners.
Warranty accruals and impact on gross margins Apple accrued a significantly lower amount of warranty accruals compared to a year ago. In the December 2016 quarter, there was $2.3 billion of accruals, or 3.0% of revenue. In the latest quarter, the amount was $1.5 billion, or 1.7% of revenue.
When you add the company’s warranty accruals back to the reported gross margin, it provides some insight into the cost of producing its products. For the December 2016 quarter, the adjusted gross margin was 41.5% versus last quarter’s 40.1%.
There are at least two takeaways from the lower warranty accruals and gross margin. The first is that even with a $999 and $1,149 iPhone X the margins were not higher, as typically, higher-priced items tend to have higher margins. The second is that the battery issue where Apple is only charging $29 to replace them did not drive a higher warranty expense .
Geographies Apple provides details for the operating profit for its five geographic regions. It is worthwhile to monitor the year-to-year trends and, to a lesser degree, which regions are more or less profitable.
The total operating margin includes expenses for research & development and various corporate expenses, which the geographies do not. Therefore, the total operating margin is lower when compared to the geographies.
Total operating margin 
December 2016 to December 2017 quarter: Flat at 29.8% The Americas, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific saw their operating margins decline year over year. Europe and Greater China had increases.
Operating profit margins (December 2016 to December 2017 quarter) 
Americas: 32.8% down 0.6% to 32.2% Europe: 31.0% up 1.7% to 32.7% Greater China: 38.0% up 0.5% to 38.5% Japan: 46.4% down 3.8% to 42.6% Rest of Asia Pacific: 38.0% down 0.4% to 37.6% Other income Apple’s cash and investments generated $1.45 billion in interest income with a return of 2.11%. Its interest expense increased from $525 million a year ago to $734 million in the December quarter. The company doesn’t provide a blended rate for its interest expense, but when you divide the interest expense into an average of last quarter’s and the current quarter’s debt, it is approximately 2.5%.
Capital expenditures Apple’s capital plan remained $16 billion for fiscal 2018, of which $2.2 billion was spent in the first fiscal quarter. This compares to $14.9 billion for all of fiscal 2017. Since the company has generated over $63 billion in operating cash flow the past two years, it can easily handle this level of capital expenditure.
Manufacturing purchase obligations Apple buys components from its suppliers. In this regard, its 10-Q says, “The Company utilizes several outsourcing partners to manufacture sub-assemblies for the Company’s products and to perform final assembly and testing of finished products. These outsourcing partners acquire components and build product based on demand information supplied by the Company, which typically covers periods up to 150 days.”
A year ago, Apple had committed to buy $24 billion worth of components and products from its suppliers, and at the end of the September quarter, it was $37.6 billion. While it decreased from the September quarter to $33.5 billion at the end of December, it did increase 40% year over year. The higher level may be due to buying components that management thinks may be in tight supply or excess inventory that needs to be worked off. It will probably take a couple of quarters to tell which one it is.
March share count could drop by 60 million I track the number of actual shares that are outstanding about three weeks after the quarter ends to get a feel on what the diluted share count used for the EPS calculation could fall to in the current quarter. It isn’t an exact correlation, but can be fairly accurate.
The number of common shares outstanding as of January 19 was 5.074 billion, down 60 million from 5.134 billion on October 20, 2017. Based on historical trends using this is a reasonable decrease in the number of diluted shares in the March quarter. There were 5.158 billion diluted shares in the December quarter, so the March quarter number should be just under 5.1 billion.
This is before Apple does a large buyback with its overseas cash that could add $32 to the share price .
